case_study_insert.main_stem: Marlowe Meadows Glamping (MMG) is a partnership in the leisure and glamping sector, employing a workforce of 16. Founded in 2019 by Sam and Priya Whitmore, the business operates a meadow site with safari tents, a communal kitchen and guided nature walks, with a flat structure and democratic leadership. MMG plans to invest $480,000 in 12 new safari tents and a meadow kitchen, financed by a $330,000 ten-year bank loan and a $150,000 hire purchase agreement. It has fixed costs of $90,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $32, and currently produces 12,000 units a year. MMG faces two operational problems: labour turnover among cleaners has reached 25% and customer complaints about Wi-Fi and noise after dark are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Advertisement and Review Extract — Summer 2025: The peak season hosted 3,100 tent-nights at an average occupancy of 82% across weekends. Customer complaints fell from 21 to 9 per month, and the site averages 4.5 out of 5 across 400 review-site ratings. A survey of 380 guests found that 57% would pay up to $10 more per night for a hot-tub upgrade, and 44% check a site's eco credentials before booking. Off-the-job customer service courses at the county college cost $550 per employee for the 10 cleaning and front-of-site staff.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marlowe Meadows Glamping as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, increasing costs for variable-rate loans and hire purchase agreements. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.20 to $12.87 per hour from April 2026, raising cleaner and kitchen wage bills. (3) Canvas, timber and energy input costs have risen 15.4% year-on-year, staycation inflation is running at 7.2%, and consumer spending on UK staycations and rural breaks grew 4.9% in the same period.

questions.question_text: MMG plans to finance its 12 new safari tents partly with a $150,000 hire purchase agreement. Explain two advantages for MMG of using hire purchase to acquire the safari tents instead of financing them from the $330,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the cost of the 12 safari tents over their working life, so MMG keeps more of the $330,000 bank loan for the meadow kitchen build and other cash needs. Repayments are predictable, ownership passes to the partnership at the end of the term, and the tents start generating revenue during the 82% peak-weekend occupancy season rather than waiting for cash to accumulate.

Point 2: Hire purchase is secured on the tents themselves, so MMG avoids over-burdening the bank loan with assets that lose value quickly. It preserves working capital for the rising 15.4% canvas, timber and energy input costs and protects the partners' ownership structure without new external investors, while the fixed repayment schedule keeps the flat structure's budgeting discipline simple for a 16-person team.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Marlowe Meadows Glamping and its safari-tent expansion decision.

questions.question_text: MMG is launching its 12 new safari tents with meadow kitchen. Consider outdoor and adventure magazine print features, partnerships with countryside holiday platforms, or a social media campaign with glamping and nature influencers. Which should MMG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Outdoor magazine print features: Long-lead features in countryside and outdoor magazines would reach an affluent rural-break readership that trusts specialist print, suiting MMG's meadow positioning. However, print lead times are long, the readership skews older and car-owning, and much of the circulation sits far beyond viable driving distance, so cost per confirmed booking could be high for a 16-person partnership funding a $480,000 expansion.

Countryside holiday platform partnerships: Listing the 12 tents on established glamping and staycation platforms places MMG directly in front of guests already searching for rural tent breaks, matching the 4.9% growth in UK staycations and the 57% of 380 surveyed guests willing to pay up to $10 more for a hot-tub upgrade. Platform commission applies, but MMG gains measurable bookings at low fixed cost.

Glamping influencer campaign: Partnering with glamping and nature influencers produces trackable, visual content — tents at dusk, meadow walks, the kitchen — targeted at the 44% of guests who check eco credentials, building national awareness cheaply. Results build slowly and depend on influencer credibility, and may attract sightseeing clicks rather than committed multi-night bookings.

Recommendation: MMG should choose partnerships with countryside holiday platforms. They convert active staycation demand into confirmed multi-night bookings, reinforce the 4.5-out-of-5 review base and the $10 hot-tub premium, and keep MMG's marketing variable with success. Magazine print is rejected as too slow and narrow for a single-season launch; influencer campaigns are rejected as too unreliable as the primary channel for a $480,000 commitment, and can be layered in later to amplify platform listings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MMG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MMG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MMG with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print and influencer campaigns are rejected as the primary channel.

questions.question_text: MMG's small team relies heavily on seasonal cleaners. Explain two benefits for MMG of using profit sharing to improve motivation among its cleaning and front-of-site staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Profit sharing gives MMG's 16 employees a direct financial stake in hitting occupancy and review targets, satisfying their need to share in the business's success (Herzberg's motivator factors) and encouraging effort beyond basic duties. Cleaners who keep the tents spotless push the 4.5-out-of-5 average higher, which directly lifts repeat bookings and weekend occupancy at 82%.

Point 2: Profit sharing signals that the partners value the whole team, not just them, which builds loyalty and reduces the 25% labour turnover among cleaners — saving the $550 per employee off-the-job customer service course cost for the 10 front-of-site staff. Lower turnover and higher morale also protect service during the noisy-after-dark problem, as engaged staff are more likely to solve guest issues proactively rather than ignore them.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MMG's turnover, reviews and expansion.

questions.question_text: MMG faces rising complaints about Wi-Fi and noise after dark. Consider hiring additional full-time front-of-site staff, or contracting a specialist quiet-hours and connectivity service. Which should MMG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Hiring full-time front-of-site staff: Permanent staff can enforce quiet hours in person, manage Wi-Fi support and greet guests, building relationships that reduce noise complaints and raise the review average beyond 4.5 out of 5. However, permanent hires add fixed salary costs to a small 16-person team, may be under-used in the off-season, and need training in connectivity troubleshooting as well as hospitality duties.

Contracting a specialist quiet-hours and connectivity service: An external specialist installs and monitors Wi-Fi, soundscaping and noise-management protocols, often with faster fix times and guaranteed service levels. Costs are mostly variable, and the service can be scaled up for the peak 82%-occupancy season, but it lacks the personal touch, may feel impersonal to luxury-minded guests, and creates dependence on an outside supplier.

Decision: MMG should hire one full-time front-of-site host for the season, supported by short-term specialist Wi-Fi installation. In-house staffing addresses both root causes — noise behaviour and guest communication — and builds the loyalty needed to reverse the 25% cleaner turnover, while the one-off Wi-Fi contract fixes the technical problem permanently. Full reliance on an external service is rejected because it would not handle the interpersonal noise issue, would weaken MMG's flat, democratic culture, and would cost more across repeat seasons than one trained employee.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to MMG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of MMG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of MMG with a well-justified decision covering cost, control and guest experience.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MMG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $90,000 ÷ ($32 − $14) = $90,000 ÷ $18 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $32 − $14 = $18.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $18.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MMG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 5,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 12,000 units to confirm the glamping site is profitably above break-even, with a margin of safety of 7,000 units, informing whether the 12 new tents can be sold out in peak weeks.
2. Contribution per unit of $18.00 lets MMG model the effect of the $10 hot-tub upgrade, for example bundling it free would cut contribution to $8.00, letting managers judge whether extra tent-nights would still cover the $90,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $90,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the booking volumes needed to justify the $330,000 bank loan repayments and the $150,000 hire purchase schedule, and to check the tents service them before committing further spend.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($90,000 ÷ 12,000 units + $14 = $21.50 a unit) to benchmark seasonal performance, identify purchasing waste behind Wi-Fi and maintenance complaints, and decide whether to renegotiate the $14 variable cost with canvas, timber and energy suppliers amid the 15.4% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $18.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 12,000-unit output; hot-tub bundle modelling vs $90,000 fixed costs; loan and hire purchase feasibility for the $480,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $21.50 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MMG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MMG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.47 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.43 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.69 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $18,000 inventories + $12,000 trade receivables + $14,000 cash = $44,000; 2025 = $26,000 + $15,000 + $9,000 = $50,000. Liquidity 2024 = $44,000 ÷ $30,000 = 1.47; 2025 = $50,000 ÷ $35,000 = 1.43. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($44,000 − $18,000) ÷ $30,000 = $26,000 ÷ $30,000 = 0.87; 2025 = ($50,000 − $26,000) ÷ $35,000 = $24,000 ÷ $35,000 = 0.69.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. The 2025 liquidity figure slipped from 1.47 to 1.43, meaning current assets cover current liabilities slightly less comfortably, helped by cash falling from $14,000 to $9,000 and current liabilities rising from $30,000 to $35,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, fell sharply from 0.87 to 0.69, so MMG is increasingly reliant on selling stock — critical while it services a $330,000 bank loan and a $150,000 hire purchase agreement for a $480,000 expansion. Inventories rose from $18,000 to $26,000, tying up cash that could have funded the meadow kitchen, and trade receivables rose from $12,000 to $15,000; if agency and platform partners pay late, short-term pressure will intensify.

Conclusion: MMG's financial position has not improved. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.47 to 1.43, and 0.87 to 0.69) show weaker short-term solvency, and the decline does not rest on inventory alone. The main risks are falling cash and rising current liabilities, so MMG should slow tent spending, tighten deposit terms on platform bookings, clear the inventory backlog before winter, and renegotiate the hire purchase schedule before drawing further on the loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether MMG's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MMG of installing solar-powered safari tents with composting toilets for its new expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Solar-powered, off-grid tents match the preferences of the 44% of 380 surveyed guests who check a site's eco credentials, and allow MMG to charge a premium that protects its $18.00 contribution per unit even as energy costs rise 15.4%. They also let MMG market a fully off-grid meadow experience, reinforcing the 4.5-out-of-5 review base and helping the 12 new tents win staycation platform listings for the $480,000 expansion.

Disadvantage: Solar and composting systems carry high upfront capital and specialist maintenance costs inside the $480,000 budget, and output is weather-dependent. If panels underperform in overcast weeks, lighting and Wi-Fi heating suffer, the $10 hot-tub premium loses appeal, and the rising Wi-Fi and noise complaints could worsen rather than fall — undermining the 4.5-out-of-5 rating that the whole eco positioning depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MMG's research data, costs and safari-tent expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase to $12.87 per hour, and the 15.4% rise in canvas, timber and energy input costs will affect MMG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): A 0.5% rise on MMG's variable-rate $330,000 ten-year bank loan and the $150,000 hire purchase agreement adds roughly $2,400 a year to financing costs. Higher rates may also weigh on consumer discretionary spend on rural breaks, though staycation spending still grew 4.9%. The direct effect is small and can be managed by fixing rates on renewal or pre-paying against the loan from summer surpluses.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.87 per hour): With 16 employees, mainly cleaners, kitchen and front-of-site roles, the rise lifts a large share of the wage bill. Roughly 10 minimum-wage staff, each working about 1,100 seasonal hours a year, would see about $12.87 × 1,100 × 5.5% ≈ $779 extra a year per worker, or roughly $7,800 across those roles — manageable through profit-sharing discipline and modest price adjustments.

Input cost inflation (15.4% canvas, timber and energy): MMG's $14 variable cost is dominated by canvas, timber and energy — roughly $10 per tent-night. A 15.4% rise on that portion adds about $1.54 per unit; at 12,000 units that is roughly $18,500 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $18.00 toward $16.46 and reducing profit, though MMG can partially recover through the $10 hot-tub premium and advance canvas and timber purchases before further rises.

Conclusion: The 15.4% rise in canvas, timber and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. It directly and repeatedly erodes the $18.00 contribution on every one of the 12,000 units sold, totalling roughly $18,500 a year — more than double the minimum-wage effect and far above the $2,400 interest-rate increase — and it strikes the very materials the $480,000 expansion depends on. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious risk at roughly $7,800, while the interest-rate rise is smallest and can be managed by fixing rates; all three still require MMG to review tent-night pricing before the April wage change.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MMG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MMG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MMG with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
